Receives data on the socket from the remote address to which it is connected, without removing that data from the queue. On success, returns the number of bytes peeked.

Successive calls return the same data. This is accomplished by passing
`MSG_PEEK` as a flag to the underlying `recv` system call.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
let stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8000")
                       .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
let mut buf = [0; 10];
let len = stream.peek(&mut buf).expect("peek failed");
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/std/net/tcp.rs.html#451)`tcp_linger`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/std/net/tcp.rs.html#451)

`tcp_linger`)Sets the value of the `SO_LINGER` option on this socket.

This value controls how the socket is closed when data remains
to be sent. If `SO_LINGER` is set, the socket will remain open
for the specified duration as the system attempts to send pending data.
Otherwise, the system may close the socket immediately, or wait for a
default timeout.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
#![feature(tcp_linger)]
use std::net::TcpStream;
use std::time::Duration;
let stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8080")
                       .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
stream.set_linger(Some(Duration::from_secs(0))).expect("set_linger call failed");
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/std/net/tcp.rs.html#473)`tcp_linger`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/std/net/tcp.rs.html#473)

`tcp_linger`)Gets the value of the `SO_LINGER` option on this socket.

For more information about this option, see [ TcpStream::set_linger](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/net/tcp/struct.TcpStream.html#method.set_linger).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
#![feature(tcp_linger)]
use std::net::TcpStream;
use std::time::Duration;
let stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8080")
                       .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
stream.set_linger(Some(Duration::from_secs(0))).expect("set_linger call failed");
assert_eq!(stream.linger().unwrap(), Some(Duration::from_secs(0)));
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/std/net/tcp.rs.html#503)#### pub fn [set_keepalive](https://docs.rs#method.set_keepalive)(&self, keepalive: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html)>

`tcp_keepalive`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/std/net/tcp.rs.html#503)

#### pub fn [set_keepalive](https://docs.rs#method.set_keepalive)(&self, keepalive: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html)>

`tcp_keepalive`)Sets the value of the `SO_KEEPALIVE` option on this socket.

If set to `true`, the operating system will periodically send keepalive
probes on an idle connection to verify that the remote peer is still
reachable. If the peer fails to respond after a system-determined number
of probes, the connection is considered broken and subsequent I/O calls
will return an error.

This is useful for detecting dead peers on long-lived connections where no application-level traffic is exchanged, such as database or SSH connections.

The timing and frequency of keepalive probes are controlled by system-level settings and are not configured by this method alone.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
#![feature(tcp_keepalive)]
use std::net::TcpStream;
let stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8080")
                       .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
stream.set_keepalive(true).expect("set_keepalive call failed");
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/std/net/tcp.rs.html#524)`tcp_keepalive`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/std/net/tcp.rs.html#524)

`tcp_keepalive`)Gets the value of the `SO_KEEPALIVE` option on this socket.

For more information about this option, see [ TcpStream::set_keepalive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/net/tcp/struct.TcpStream.html#method.set_keepalive).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
#![feature(tcp_keepalive)]
use std::net::TcpStream;
let stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8080")
                       .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
stream.set_keepalive(true).expect("set_keepalive call failed");
assert_eq!(stream.keepalive().unwrap_or(false), true);
```
Sets the value of the `TCP_NODELAY` option on this socket.

If set, this option disables the Nagle algorithm. This means that segments are always sent as soon as possible, even if there is only a small amount of data. When not set, data is buffered until there is a sufficient amount to send out, thereby avoiding the frequent sending of small packets.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
let stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8080")
                       .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
stream.set_nodelay(true).expect("set_nodelay call failed");
```
Gets the value of the `TCP_NODELAY` option on this socket.

For more information about this option, see [ TcpStream::set_nodelay](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/net/tcp/struct.TcpStream.html#method.set_nodelay).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
let stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8080")
                       .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
stream.set_nodelay(true).expect("set_nodelay call failed");
assert_eq!(stream.nodelay().unwrap_or(false), true);
```
Sets the value for the `IP_TTL` option on this socket.

This value sets the time-to-live field that is used in every packet sent from this socket.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
let stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8080")
                       .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
stream.set_ttl(100).expect("set_ttl call failed");
```
Gets the value of the `IP_TTL` option for this socket.

For more information about this option, see [ TcpStream::set_ttl](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/net/tcp/struct.TcpStream.html#method.set_ttl).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
let stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8080")
                       .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
stream.set_ttl(100).expect("set_ttl call failed");
assert_eq!(stream.ttl().unwrap_or(0), 100);
```
Gets the value of the `SO_ERROR` option on this socket.

This will retrieve the stored error in the underlying socket, clearing the field in the process. This can be useful for checking errors between calls.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
let stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8080")
                       .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
stream.take_error().expect("No error was expected...");
```
Moves this TCP stream into or out of nonblocking mode.

This will result in `read`, `write`, `recv` and `send` system operations
becoming nonblocking, i.e., immediately returning from their calls.
If the IO operation is successful, `Ok` is returned and no further
action is required. If the IO operation could not be completed and needs
to be retried, an error with kind [ io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/io/error/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.WouldBlock) is
returned.

On most Unix platforms, calling this method corresponds to calling `ioctl`
`FIONBIO`. On Windows, calling this method corresponds to calling
`ioctlsocket` `FIONBIO`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

Reading bytes from a TCP stream in non-blocking mode:

```
use std::io::{self, Read};
use std::net::TcpStream;
let mut stream = TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:7878")
    .expect("Couldn't connect to the server...");
stream.set_nonblocking(true).expect("set_nonblocking call failed");
let mut buf = vec![];
loop {
    match stream.read_to_end(&mut buf) {
        Ok(_) => break,
        Err(ref e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::WouldBlock => {
            // wait until network socket is ready, typically implemented
            // via platform-specific APIs such as epoll or IOCP
            wait_for_fd();
        }
        Err(e) => panic!("encountered IO error: {e}"),
    };
};
println!("bytes: {buf:?}");
```

# NativeTlsConnector in amq_protocol_tcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-tcp/10.6.2/amq_protocol_tcp/struct.NativeTlsConnector.html

`pub struct NativeTlsConnector(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A builder for client-side TLS connections.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use native_tls::TlsConnector;
use std::io::{Read, Write};
use std::net::TcpStream;
let connector = TlsConnector::new().unwrap();
let stream = TcpStream::connect("google.com:443").unwrap();
let mut stream = connector.connect("google.com", stream).unwrap();
stream.write_all(b"GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n").unwrap();
let mut res = vec![];
stream.read_to_end(&mut res).unwrap();
println!("{}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&res));
```

#### pub fn [connect](https://docs.rs#method.connect)<S>(
    &self,
    domain: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    stream: S,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[TlsStream](https://docs.rs/native-tls/0.2.18/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/native_tls/struct.TlsStream.html)<S>, [HandshakeError](https://docs.rs/native-tls/0.2.18/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/native_tls/enum.HandshakeError.html)<S>>

Initiates a TLS handshake.

The provided domain will be used for both SNI and certificate hostname validation.

If the socket is nonblocking and a `WouldBlock` error is returned during
the handshake, a `HandshakeError::WouldBlock` error will be returned
which can be used to restart the handshake when the socket is ready
again.

The domain is ignored if both SNI and hostname verification are disabled.

# OpensslConnector in amq_protocol_tcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-tcp/10.6.2/amq_protocol_tcp/struct.OpensslConnector.html

`pub struct OpensslConnector(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A type which wraps client-side streams in a TLS session.

OpenSSL’s default configuration is highly insecure. This connector manages the OpenSSL structures, configuring cipher suites, session options, hostname verification, and more.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

**AMQP 0-9-1 protocol codec and TCP/TLS connection layer for Rust.**

This workspace provides the low-level AMQP 0-9-1 building blocks used by

# async-rs 0.8.11 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-rs/^0.8

**A Rust async runtime abstraction library.**

Provides a unified `Runtime` enum and a `traits` module (`Executor`, `Reactor`,
`Dns`, …) that abstract over Tokio, smol, and async-global-executor.
Applications select exactly one runtime via feature flags; library crates
depend on the trait objects and remain runtime-agnostic.

## Feature flags

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `tokio`(default) | Tokio runtime |
| `smol` | smol executor |
| `async-global-executor` | async-global-executor |
| `async-io` | async-io reactor (required by `smol`) |
| `hickory-dns` | Hickory DNS resolver (tokio only) |

## Example

```
use ;
use ;
async
async
async
```

# tcp-stream 0.34.14 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/tcp-stream/^0.34.5

**A **`TcpStream` with pluggable TLS support.

Wraps `std::net::TcpStream` in a `TcpStream` enum that can be upgraded to a
TLS-encrypted stream via `TcpStream::into_tls`. Supported backends are rustls
(default), native-tls, and OpenSSL. Async `futures-io` trait implementations
are provided when the `futures` feature is enabled.

| `openssl` | TLS via OpenSSL |

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls-platform-verifier`*(default)* | Uses the platform trust store |
| `rustls-native-certs` | Loads native root certificates |
| `rustls-webpki-roots-certs` | Uses the webpki bundled root set |

### Rustls crypto provider (at least one required)

| Flag | Notes |

| `vendored-openssl` | Build a vendored OpenSSL (requires `openssl`feature) |

# tracing 0.1.44 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/tracing/^0.1

# tracing

Application-level tracing for Rust.

## Overview

`tracing` is a framework for instrumenting Rust programs to collect
structured, event-based diagnostic information.

In asynchronous systems like Tokio, interpreting traditional log messages can
often be quite challenging. Since individual tasks are multiplexed on the same
thread, associated events and log lines are intermixed making it difficult to
trace the logic flow. `tracing` expands upon logging-style diagnostics by
allowing libraries and applications to record structured events with additional
information about *temporality* and *causality* — unlike a log message, a span
in `tracing` has a beginning and end time, may be entered and exited by the
flow of execution, and may exist within a nested tree of similar spans. In
addition, `tracing` spans are *structured*, with the ability to record typed
data as well as textual messages.

The `tracing` crate provides the APIs necessary for instrumenting libraries
and applications to emit trace data.

*Compiler support:  requires *

`rustc` 1.65+## Usage

(The examples below are borrowed from the `log` crate's yak-shaving
[example](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.10/log/index.html#examples), modified to
idiomatic `tracing`.)

### In Applications

In order to record trace events, executables have to use a `Subscriber`
implementation compatible with `tracing`. A `Subscriber` implements a way of
collecting trace data, such as by logging it to standard output. [ tracing_subscriber](https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber/)'s

[provides reasonable defaults. Additionally,](https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber/0.3/tracing_subscriber/fmt/index.html)

`fmt` module`tracing-subscriber` is able to consume messages emitted by `log`-instrumented libraries and modules.The simplest way to use a subscriber is to call the `set_global_default` function.

```
use ;
use FmtSubscriber;
```
```
[]
 = "0.1"
 = "0.3.0"
```
This subscriber will be used as the default in all threads for the remainder of the duration
of the program, similar to how loggers work in the `log` crate.

In addition, you can locally override the default subscriber. For example:

```
use ;
use FmtSubscriber;
```
This approach allows trace data to be collected by multiple subscribers within different contexts in the program. Note that the override only applies to the currently executing thread; other threads will not see the change from with_default.

Any trace events generated outside the context of a subscriber will not be collected.

Once a subscriber has been set, instrumentation points may be added to the
executable using the `tracing` crate's macros.

### In Libraries

Libraries should only rely on the `tracing` crate and use the provided macros
and types to collect whatever information might be useful to downstream consumers.

```
use ;
use ;
// the `#[tracing::instrument]` attribute creates and enters a span
// every time the instrumented function is called. The span is named after the
// the function or method. Parameters passed to the function are recorded as fields.
```
```
[]
 = "0.1"
```
Note: Libraries should *NOT* call `set_global_default()`, as this will cause
conflicts when executables try to set the default later.

### In Asynchronous Code

If you are instrumenting code that make use of
[ std::future::Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/future/trait.Future.html)
or async/await, avoid using the

`Span::enter` method. The following example
*will not*work:

```
async
```
```
async
```
The span guard `_s` will not exit until the future generated by the `async` block is complete.
Since futures and spans can be entered and exited *multiple* times without them completing,
the span remains entered for as long as the future exists, rather than being entered only when
it is polled, leading to very confusing and incorrect output.
For more details, see [the documentation on closing spans](https://tracing.rs/tracing/span/index.html#closing-spans).

There are two ways to instrument asynchronous code. The first is through the
[ Future::instrument](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/trait.Instrument.html#method.instrument) combinator:

```
use Instrument;
let my_future = async ;
my_future
    .instrument
    .await
```
`Future::instrument` attaches a span to the future, ensuring that the span's lifetime
is as long as the future's.

The second, and preferred, option is through the
[ #[instrument]](https://docs.rs/tracing/0.1.44/tracing/attr.instrument.html)
attribute:

```
use ;
use ;
use io;
async
```
Under the hood, the `#[instrument]` macro performs the same explicit span
attachment that `Future::instrument` does.

### Concepts

This crate provides macros for creating `Span`s and `Event`s, which represent
periods of time and momentary events within the execution of a program,
respectively.

As a rule of thumb, *spans* should be used to represent discrete units of work
(e.g., a given request's lifetime in a server) or periods of time spent in a
given context (e.g., time spent interacting with an instance of an external
system, such as a database). In contrast, *events* should be used to represent
points in time within a span — a request returned with a given status code,
*n* new items were taken from a queue, and so on.

`Span`s are constructed using the `span!` macro, and then *entered*
to indicate that some code takes place within the context of that `Span`:

```
use ;
// Construct a new span named "my span".
let mut span = span!;
span.in_scope;
// Dropping the span will close it, indicating that it has ended.
```
The [ #[instrument]](https://docs.rs/tracing/0.1.44/tracing/attr.instrument.html) attribute macro
can reduce some of this boilerplate:

```
use ;
```
The `Event` type represent an event that occurs instantaneously, and is
essentially a `Span` that cannot be entered. They are created using the `event!`
macro:

```
use ;
event!;
```
Users of the [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/) crate should note that

`tracing` exposes a set of macros for
creating `Event`s (`trace!`, `debug!`, `info!`, `warn!`, and `error!`) which may
be invoked with the same syntax as the similarly-named macros from the `log`
crate. Often, the process of converting a project to use `tracing` can begin
with a simple drop-in replacement.## Supported Rust Versions

Tracing is built against the latest stable release. The minimum supported version is 1.42. The current Tracing version is not guaranteed to build on Rust versions earlier than the minimum supported version.

Tracing follows the same compiler support policies as the rest of the Tokio project. The current stable Rust compiler and the three most recent minor versions before it will always be supported. For example, if the current stable compiler version is 1.45, the minimum supported version will not be increased past 1.42, three minor versions prior. Increasing the minimum supported compiler version is not considered a semver breaking change as long as doing so complies with this policy.

## Ecosystem

### Related Crates

In addition to `tracing` and `tracing-core`, the [ tokio-rs/tracing](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing) repository
contains several additional crates designed to be used with the

`tracing` ecosystem.
This includes a collection of `Subscriber` implementations, as well as utility
and adapter crates to assist in writing `Subscriber`s and instrumenting
applications.In particular, the following crates are likely to be of interest:

- `tracing-futures`- `futures`crate, allowing spans to be attached to- `Future`s,- `Stream`s, and- `Executor`s.
- `tracing-subscriber`- `Subscriber`implementations and utilities for working with- `Subscriber`s. This includes a- `FmtSubscriber`- `FmtSubscriber`for logging formatted trace data to stdout, with similar filtering and formatting to the- `env_logger`
- `tracing-log`- `log`- `tracing`- `Event`s within the trace tree. This is useful when a project using- `tracing`have dependencies which use- `log`. Note that if you're using- `tracing-subscriber`'s- `FmtSubscriber`, you don't need to depend on- `tracing-log`directly.

Additionally, there are also several third-party crates which are not
maintained by the `tokio` project. These include:

- `tracing-timing`- `tracing`. It provides a subscriber that records the time elapsed between pairs of- `tracing`events and generates histograms.
- `tracing-opentelemetry`- [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/)-compatible distributed tracing systems.
- `tracing-honeycomb`- [honeycomb.io](https://www.honeycomb.io/). Backed by- `tracing-distributed`
- `tracing-distributed`
- `tracing-actix`- `tracing`integration for the- `actix`actor framework.
- `axum-insights`- `tracing`integration and Application insights export for the- `axum`web framework.
- `tracing-gelf`
- `tracing-coz`- [coz](https://github.com/plasma-umass/coz)causal profiler (Linux-only).
- `test-log`- `tracing`for tests, based on environment variables with an- `env_logger`compatible syntax.
- `tracing-unwrap`- `Result`or- `Option`types to a- `Subscriber`.
- `diesel-tracing`- `diesel`
- `tracing-tracy`- [Tracy](https://github.com/wolfpld/tracy)profiles in instrumented applications.
- `tracing-elastic-apm`- [Elastic APM](https://www.elastic.co/apm).
- `tracing-etw`- [ETW](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/etw/about-event-tracing)events.
- `tracing-fluent-assertions`- `tracing`spans.
- `sentry-tracing`- [Sentry](https://sentry.io/welcome/).
- `tracing-loki`- [Grafana Loki](https://grafana.com/oss/loki/).
- `tracing-logfmt`
- `json-subscriber`- `FmtSubscriber`

If you're the maintainer of a `tracing` ecosystem crate not listed above,
please let us know! We'd love to add your project to the list!

**Note:** that some of the ecosystem crates are currently unreleased and
undergoing active development. They may be less stable than `tracing` and
`tracing-core`.

## Supported Rust Versions

Tracing is built against the latest stable release. The minimum supported version is 1.65. The current Tracing version is not guaranteed to build on Rust versions earlier than the minimum supported version.

Tracing follows the same compiler support policies as the rest of the Tokio project. The current stable Rust compiler and the three most recent minor versions before it will always be supported. For example, if the current stable compiler version is 1.69, the minimum supported version will not be increased past 1.66, three minor versions prior. Increasing the minimum supported compiler version is not considered a semver breaking change as long as doing so complies with this policy.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in Tokio by you, shall be licensed as MIT, without any additional terms or conditions.

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls-platform-verifier`*(default)* | Uses the platform trust store |
| `rustls-native-certs` | Loads native root certificates |
| `rustls-webpki-roots-certs` | Uses the webpki bundled root set |

### Rustls crypto provider (at least one required)

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls--aws_lc_rs`*(default)* | Uses aws-lc-rs |
| `rustls--ring` | Uses ring (more portable, e.g. builds on Windows) |

### Miscellaneous

| Flag | Notes |
| `codegen` | Force protocol code regeneration at build time |
| `verbose-errors` | More detailed AMQP parser error messages |
| `hickory-dns` | Hickory DNS resolver (avoids spurious network hangs) |

---

# amq-protocol-tcp 10.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/amq-protocol-tcp/10.6.0

**AMQP 0-9-1 protocol codec and TCP/TLS connection layer for Rust.**

This workspace provides the low-level AMQP 0-9-1 building blocks used by
[lapin](https://docs.rs/lapin). It is split into focused sub-crates that can
also be used independently.

## Crates in this workspace

Most users should depend on `amq-protocol` directly — it re-exports everything
and wires up the sub-crates. Depend on a sub-crate only when you need a strict
subset of the functionality.

## Feature flags

### Async runtime (pick exactly one)

| Flag | Notes |
| `tokio`*(default)* | Requires a running Tokio runtime |
| `smol` | Uses the smol executor |
| `async-global-executor` | Uses async-global-executor |

### TLS backend (pick at most one)

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls`*(default)* | TLS via rustls |
| `native-tls` | TLS via the platform's native library |
| `openssl` | TLS via OpenSSL |

### Rustls certificate store (when `rustls` is active)

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls-platform-verifier`*(default)* | Uses the platform trust store |
| `rustls-native-certs` | Loads native root certificates |
| `rustls-webpki-roots-certs` | Uses the webpki bundled root set |

### Rustls crypto provider (at least one required)

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls--aws_lc_rs`*(default)* | Uses aws-lc-rs |
| `rustls--ring` | Uses ring (more portable, e.g. builds on Windows) |

### Miscellaneous

| Flag | Notes |
| `codegen` | Force protocol code regeneration at build time |
| `verbose-errors` | More detailed AMQP parser error messages |
| `hickory-dns` | Hickory DNS resolver (avoids spurious network hangs) |

---

# amq-protocol-tcp 10.5.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/amq-protocol-tcp/10.5.0

## Features

- codegen: force code generation (default to pregenerated sources)
- hickory-dns: use hickory-dns for domain name resolution to avoid spurious network hangs
- vendored-openssl: use a vendored openssl version instead of the system one (when using openssl backend)
- verbose-errors: enable more verbose errors in the AMQP parser

## Runtime

- tokio (default)
- smol
- async-global-executor

## TLS backends

- native-tls
- openssl
- rustls (default)

## Rustls certificates store

- rustls-platform-verifier (default)
- rustls-native-certs
- rustls-webpki-roots-certs

## Warning about crypto backends for rustls

A crypto implementation must be enabled in rustls using feature flags. We mimic what rustls does, providing one feature flag per implementation and enabling the same as rustls by default. Available options are:

- `rustls--aws_lc_rs`(default)
- `rustls--ring`

---

# amq_protocol - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/amq-protocol

## Expand description

AMQP 0-9-1 protocol codec for Rust.

This crate is the main entry point for the `amq-protocol` workspace. It
re-exports the [ tcp](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-tcp/10.6.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_tcp/index.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-types/10.6.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_types/index.html)

`types`[sub-crates and provides the code-generated](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-uri/10.6.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_uri/index.html)

`uri`[module (produced from the RabbitMQ spec), plus](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)

`protocol`[helpers and](https://docs.rs/auth/index.html)

`auth`[serialisation/deserialisation utilities.](https://docs.rs/frame/index.html)

`frame`[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

[§](https://docs.rs#async-runtime-pick-exactly-one)Async runtime (pick exactly one)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `tokio`(default) | Requires a running Tokio runtime |
| `smol` | Uses the smol executor |
| `async-global-executor` | Uses async-global-executor |

[§](https://docs.rs#tls-backend-pick-at-most-one-rustls-is-the-default)TLS backend (pick at most one; `rustls` is the default)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls`(default) | TLS via rustls |
| `native-tls` | TLS via the platform’s native library |
| `openssl` | TLS via OpenSSL |

[§](https://docs.rs#rustls-certificate-store-only-when-rustls-is-active)Rustls certificate store (only when `rustls` is active)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls-platform-verifier`(default) | Uses the platform trust store |
| `rustls-native-certs` | Loads native root certificates |
| `rustls-webpki-roots-certs` | Uses the webpki bundled root set |

[§](https://docs.rs#rustls-crypto-provider-at-least-one-must-be-enabled)Rustls crypto provider (at least one must be enabled)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls--aws_lc_rs`(default) | Uses aws-lc-rs |
| `rustls--ring` | Uses ring (more portable) |

[§](https://docs.rs#miscellaneous)Miscellaneous

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `codegen` | Force protocol code regeneration at build time |
| `verbose-errors` | More detailed AMQP parser error messages |
| `hickory-dns` | Use hickory-dns for name resolution |

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [amq_protocol_tcp](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-tcp/10.6.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_tcp/index.html)as tcp;
- `pub use`- [amq_protocol_types](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-types/10.6.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_types/index.html)as types;
- `pub use`- [amq_protocol_uri](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-uri/10.6.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_uri/index.html)as uri;

---

# lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin

## Expand description

An async AMQP 0-9-1 client library targeting RabbitMQ.

[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core concepts

`Connection`

`Channel`[. All AMQP operations (declaring queues, publishing, consuming, …) are performed through channels. Open as many as you need; they are cheap.](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html)

`Connection`

`Consumer``Stream` of [values obtained by calling](https://docs.rs/message/struct.Delivery.html)

`message::Delivery`[. Each delivery must be explicitly acknowledged once processed.](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_consume)

`Channel::basic_consume`

`PublisherConfirm`[that resolves to a](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_publish)

`Channel::basic_publish`[once the broker has acknowledged the message (requires](https://docs.rs/enum.Confirmation.html)

`Confirmation`[).](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.confirm_select)

`Channel::confirm_select`[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use async_rs::traits::Executor;
use futures_lite::stream::StreamExt;
use lapin::{
    options::*, types::FieldTable, BasicProperties, Connection,
    ConnectionProperties, Result,
};
fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let addr = std::env::var("AMQP_ADDR")
        .unwrap_or_else(|_| "amqp://127.0.0.1:5672/%2f".into());
    let runtime = lapin::runtime::default_runtime()?;
    runtime.clone().block_on(async move {
        let conn = Connection::connect(&addr, ConnectionProperties::default()).await?;
        let channel = conn.create_channel().await?;
        channel
            .queue_declare("hello".into(), QueueDeclareOptions::durable(), FieldTable::default())
            .await?;
        channel
            .basic_publish(
                "".into(),
                "hello".into(),
                BasicPublishOptions::default(),
                b"Hello, world!",
                BasicProperties::default(),
            )
            .await?
            .await?;
        let mut consumer = channel
            .basic_consume(
                "hello".into(),
                "my_consumer".into(),
                BasicConsumeOptions::default(),
                FieldTable::default(),
            )
            .await?;
        while let Some(delivery) = consumer.next().await {
            let delivery = delivery?;
            delivery.ack(BasicAckOptions::default()).await?;
        }
        Ok(())
    })
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#automatic-connection-recovery)Automatic connection recovery

Enable recovery in [ ConnectionProperties](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionProperties.html) to automatically reconnect and
replay topology (exchanges, queues, bindings, consumers) after a network
failure:

```
use lapin::ConnectionProperties;
let props = ConnectionProperties::default().enable_auto_recover();
// then pass `props` to Connection::connect(…)
```
After catching an error from a channel operation, call
[ Channel::wait_for_recovery](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.wait_for_recovery) to block until the connection has been
re-established:

`channel.wait_for_recovery(error).await?;`[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

[§](https://docs.rs#async-runtime-pick-exactly-one)Async runtime (pick exactly one)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `tokio`(default) | Requires a Tokio runtime |
| `smol` | Uses the smol executor |
| `async-global-executor` | Uses async-global-executor |

[§](https://docs.rs#tls-backend-pick-at-most-one-rustls-is-the-default)TLS backend (pick at most one; `rustls` is the default)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls`(default) | TLS via rustls |
| `native-tls` | TLS via the platform’s native library |
| `openssl` | TLS via OpenSSL |

[§](https://docs.rs#rustls-certificate-store-only-when-rustls-is-active)Rustls certificate store (only when `rustls` is active)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls-platform-verifier`(default) | Uses the platform trust store |
| `rustls-native-certs` | Loads native root certificates |
| `rustls-webpki-roots-certs` | Uses the webpki bundled root set |

[§](https://docs.rs#rustls-crypto-provider-at-least-one-must-be-enabled)Rustls crypto provider (at least one must be enabled)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls--aws_lc_rs`(default) | Uses aws-lc-rs |
| `rustls--ring` | Uses ring (more portable) |

[§](https://docs.rs#miscellaneous)Miscellaneous

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `hickory-dns` | Use hickory-dns for name resolution |
| `codegen` | Force code regeneration at build time |
| `verbose-errors` | More detailed AMQP parser error messages |

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [auth](https://docs.rs/auth/index.html)
- Authentication providers and helpers for connecting to RabbitMQ.
- [message](https://docs.rs/message/index.html)
- AMQP message types delivered to consumers.
- [options](https://docs.rs/options/index.html)
- Options structs for every AMQP method that accepts flag arguments.
- [protocol](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)
- Code-generated AMQP 0-9-1 method and property types derived from the RabbitMQ spec.
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)
- Runtime selection and helpers.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Acker](https://docs.rs/struct.Acker.html)
- Handle for acknowledging, negatively acknowledging, or rejecting a delivery.
- [Channel](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html)
- Main entry point for most AMQP operations.
- [Channel](https://docs.rs/struct.ChannelStatus.html)- Status
- Shared, cheaply cloneable view of a channel’s current state.
- [Configuration](https://docs.rs/struct.Configuration.html)
- The negotiated connection parameters returned by the AMQP handshake.
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html)
- A TCP connection to the AMQP server.
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builder for `Connection`
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionProperties.html)- Properties
- Configuration for establishing a `Connection`
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionStatus.html)- Status
- Shared, cheaply cloneable view of a connection’s current state.
- [Consumer](https://docs.rs/struct.Consumer.html)
- Continuously consumes message from a Queue.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- The error that can be returned in this crate.
- [Publisher](https://docs.rs/struct.PublisherConfirm.html)- Confirm
- A future that resolves to the broker’s acknowledgement of a published message.
- [Queue](https://docs.rs/struct.Queue.html)
- Information about an AMQP queue as returned by the server.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/enum.AsyncTcpStream.html)- TcpStream
- Wrapper around plain or TLS async TCP streams
- [Channel](https://docs.rs/enum.ChannelState.html)- State
- The lifecycle state of an AMQP channel.
- [Confirmation](https://docs.rs/enum.Confirmation.html)
- The broker’s response to a published message.
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/enum.ConnectionState.html)- State
- The lifecycle state of an AMQP connection.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html)- Kind
- The type of error that can be returned in this crate.
- [Event](https://docs.rs/enum.Event.html)
- A connection-level event delivered via `Connection::events_listener`
- [Exchange](https://docs.rs/enum.ExchangeKind.html)- Kind
- The routing algorithm used by an AMQP exchange.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Connect](https://docs.rs/trait.Connect.html)
- Extension trait that lets URI types open a `Connection`
- [Consumer](https://docs.rs/trait.ConsumerDelegate.html)- Delegate
- Callback-based alternative to polling a `Consumer`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Basic](https://docs.rs/type.BasicProperties.html)- Properties
- Type alias for AMQP BasicProperties
- [Default](https://docs.rs/type.DefaultConnectionBuilder.html)- Connection - Builder
- A `ConnectionBuilder`
- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A std Result with a lapin::Error error type

# amq_protocol_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-types

## Expand description

AMQP 0-9-1 type system for Rust.

Implements the full set of AMQP scalar types ([ AMQPValue](https://docs.rs/enum.AMQPValue.html),

[), compound types (](https://docs.rs/enum.AMQPType.html)

`AMQPType`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldTable.html)

`FieldTable`[), and wire-format serialisation/deserialisation via the](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldArray.html)

`FieldArray`[and](https://docs.rs/generation/index.html)

`generation`[modules.](https://docs.rs/parsing/index.html)

`parsing`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [flags](https://docs.rs/flags/index.html)
- Helpers to handle AMQP flags.
- [generation](https://docs.rs/generation/index.html)
- Generation utilities for the various AMQP types.
- [parsing](https://docs.rs/parsing/index.html)
- Parsing utilities for the various AMQP types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Byte](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteArray.html)- Array
- An array of bytes (RabbitMQ specific)
- [Decimal](https://docs.rs/struct.DecimalValue.html)- Value
- A Decimal value composed of a scale and a value
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldArray.html)- Array
- An array of AMQPValue
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldTable.html)- Table
- A Map<String, AMQPValue>
- [Long](https://docs.rs/struct.LongString.html)- String
- A String
- [Short](https://docs.rs/struct.ShortString.html)- String
- A String (deprecated)
- [Short](https://docs.rs/struct.ShortStringError.html)- String - Error
- Error returned when constructing a [ShortString](https://docs.rs/struct.ShortString.html)from a string that exceeds[MAX_SHORT_STRING_LENGTH](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_SHORT_STRING_LENGTH.html)

# amq_protocol_tcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-tcp

## Expand description

TCP/TLS connection helpers for AMQP URIs.

Provides [ AMQPUriTcpExt](https://docs.rs/trait.AMQPUriTcpExt.html), a trait that extends

[with a](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-uri/10.6.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_uri/struct.AMQPUri.html)

`AMQPUri`[method that opens a](https://docs.rs/trait.AMQPUriTcpExt.html#method.connect)

`connect`[— with or without TLS — according to the URI scheme and the active runtime/TLS feature flags.](https://docs.rs/enum.TcpStream.html)

`TcpStream`[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

[§](https://docs.rs#async-runtime-pick-exactly-one)Async runtime (pick exactly one)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `tokio`(default) | Requires a running Tokio runtime |
| `smol` | Uses the smol executor |
| `async-global-executor` | Uses async-global-executor |

[§](https://docs.rs#tls-backend-pick-at-most-one-rustls-is-the-default)TLS backend (pick at most one; `rustls` is the default)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls`(default) | TLS via rustls |
| `native-tls` | TLS via the platform’s native library |
| `openssl` | TLS via OpenSSL |

[§](https://docs.rs#rustls-certificate-store-only-when-rustls-is-active)Rustls certificate store (only when `rustls` is active)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls-platform-verifier`(default) | Uses the platform trust store |
| `rustls-native-certs` | Loads native root certificates |
| `rustls-webpki-roots-certs` | Uses the webpki bundled root set |

[§](https://docs.rs#rustls-crypto-provider-at-least-one-must-be-enabled)Rustls crypto provider (at least one must be enabled)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls--aws_lc_rs`(default) | Uses aws-lc-rs |
| `rustls--ring` | Uses ring (more portable) |

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Native](https://docs.rs/struct.NativeTlsConnector.html)- TlsConnector
- A builder for client-side TLS connections.
- [Openssl](https://docs.rs/struct.OpensslConnector.html)- Connector
- A type which wraps client-side streams in a TLS session.
- [OwnedTLS](https://docs.rs/struct.OwnedTLSConfig.html)- Config
- Re-export TcpStream Holds extra TLS configuration
- [Rustls](https://docs.rs/struct.RustlsConnector.html)- Connector
- A rustls TLS connector ready to perform TLS handshakes.
- [Rustls](https://docs.rs/struct.RustlsConnectorConfig.html)- Connector - Config
- Configuration helper for `RustlsConnector`
- [TLSConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.TLSConfig.html)
- Re-export TcpStream Holds extra TLS configuration

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/enum.AsyncTcpStream.html)- TcpStream
- Re-export TcpStream Wrapper around plain or TLS async TCP streams
- [Handshake](https://docs.rs/enum.HandshakeError.html)- Error
- Re-export TcpStream An error returned while performing the handshake
- [Identity](https://docs.rs/enum.Identity.html)
- Re-export TcpStream Holds one of:
- [MidHandshake](https://docs.rs/enum.MidHandshakeTlsStream.html)- TlsStream
- Re-export TcpStream A TLS stream which has been interrupted during the handshake
- [Owned](https://docs.rs/enum.OwnedIdentity.html)- Identity
- Re-export TcpStream Holds one of:
- [TcpStream](https://docs.rs/enum.TcpStream.html)
- Re-export TcpStream Wrapper around plain or TLS TCP streams

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/trait.AMQPUriTcpExt.html)- UriTcp - Ext
- Trait providing a method to connect to a TcpStream

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Handshake](https://docs.rs/type.HandshakeResult.html)- Result
- Re-export TcpStream
Holds either the TLS `TcpStream`result or the current handshake state

# amq_protocol_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-codegen

## Expand description

Code generation utilities for the AMQP 0-9-1 specification.

Parses the RabbitMQ machine-readable protocol spec and exposes a
[Handlebars](https://docs.rs/handlebars)-based templating engine so that
build scripts can generate Rust source code from it. Used internally by
the `amq-protocol` and `lapin` build scripts.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/struct.AMQPClass.html)- Class
- A class as defined in the AMQP specification
- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/struct.AMQPConstant.html)- Constant
- A constant as defined in the AMQP specification
- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/struct.AMQPFlagArgument.html)- Flag - Argument
- An argument holding a flag as defined in the AMQP specification
- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/struct.AMQPFlagsArgument.html)- Flags - Argument
- An argument holding a flags as defined in the AMQP specification
- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/struct.AMQPMethod.html)- Method
- A method as defined in the AMQP specification
- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/struct.AMQPProperty.html)- Property
- A property as defined in the AMQP specification
- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/struct.AMQPValueArgument.html)- Value - Argument
- An argument holding a value as defined in the AMQP specification
- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/struct.AMQPValueRefHelper.html)- Value - RefHelper
- Helper for “unwrapping” an amqp_value
- [AMQProtocol](https://docs.rs/struct.AMQProtocolDefinition.html)- Definition
- Structure holding the definition of the protocol
- [Camel](https://docs.rs/struct.CamelHelper.html)- Helper
- Helper for converting text to camel case
- [Each](https://docs.rs/struct.EachArgumentHelper.html)- Argument - Helper
- Helper to walk through a Vec of [AMQPArgument](https://docs.rs/specs.AMQPArgument.html).
- [Include](https://docs.rs/struct.IncludeMoreHelper.html)- More - Helper
- Helper to include additional code such as rustdoc
- [Pass](https://docs.rs/struct.PassByRefHelper.html)- ByRef - Helper
- Helper to check whether a param is passed by ref or not
- [Sanitize](https://docs.rs/struct.SanitizeNameHelper.html)- Name - Helper
- Helper to sanitize name so the it becomes a valid identifier
- [Snake](https://docs.rs/struct.SnakeHelper.html)- Helper
- Helper for converting text to snake case
- [Snake](https://docs.rs/struct.SnakeTypeHelper.html)- Type - Helper
- Helper for getting the type name converted to snake case
- [UseBytes](https://docs.rs/struct.UseBytesRefHelper.html)- RefHelper
- Helper to check whether a param is passed using an &[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)or its real type
- [UseStr](https://docs.rs/struct.UseStrRefHelper.html)- RefHelper
- Helper to check whether a param is passed using an &str or its real type

```
[![API Docs](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol)
[![Build status](https://github.com/amqp-rs/amq-protocol/workflows/Build%20and%20test/badge.svg)](https://github.com/amqp-rs/amq-protocol/actions)
[![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/crates/d/amq-protocol.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/amq-protocol)

[![LICENSE](https://img.shields.io/crates/l/amq-protocol)](LICENSE)
**AMQP 0-9-1 protocol codec and TCP/TLS connection layer for Rust.**
This workspace provides the low-level AMQP 0-9-1 building blocks used by
[lapin](https://docs.rs/lapin). It is split into focused sub-crates that can
also be used independently.
Most users should depend on `amq-protocol` directly — it re-exports everything
and wires up the sub-crates. Depend on a sub-crate only when you need a strict
subset of the functionality.
```

# amq-protocol-uri 10.6.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/amq-protocol-uri/10.6.2

**AMQP 0-9-1 protocol codec and TCP/TLS connection layer for Rust.**

This workspace provides the low-level AMQP 0-9-1 building blocks used by
[lapin](https://docs.rs/lapin). It is split into focused sub-crates that can
also be used independently.

## Crates in this workspace

Most users should depend on `amq-protocol` directly — it re-exports everything
and wires up the sub-crates. Depend on a sub-crate only when you need a strict
subset of the functionality.

## Feature flags

### Async runtime (pick exactly one)

| Flag | Notes |
| `tokio`*(default)* | Requires a running Tokio runtime |
| `smol` | Uses the smol executor |
| `async-global-executor` | Uses async-global-executor |

### TLS backend (pick at most one)

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls`*(default)* | TLS via rustls |
| `native-tls` | TLS via the platform's native library |
| `openssl` | TLS via OpenSSL |

### Rustls certificate store (when `rustls` is active)

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls-platform-verifier`*(default)* | Uses the platform trust store |
| `rustls-native-certs` | Loads native root certificates |
| `rustls-webpki-roots-certs` | Uses the webpki bundled root set |

### Rustls crypto provider (at least one required)

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls--aws_lc_rs`*(default)* | Uses aws-lc-rs |
| `rustls--ring` | Uses ring (more portable, e.g. builds on Windows) |

### Miscellaneous

| Flag | Notes |
| `codegen` | Force protocol code regeneration at build time |
| `verbose-errors` | More detailed AMQP parser error messages |
| `hickory-dns` | Hickory DNS resolver (avoids spurious network hangs) |

---

# amq_protocol_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-types/=10.6.2/

## Expand description

AMQP 0-9-1 type system for Rust.

Implements the full set of AMQP scalar types ([ AMQPValue](https://docs.rs/enum.AMQPValue.html),

[), compound types (](https://docs.rs/enum.AMQPType.html)

`AMQPType`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldTable.html)

`FieldTable`[), and wire-format serialisation/deserialisation via the](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldArray.html)

`FieldArray`[and](https://docs.rs/generation/index.html)

`generation`[modules.](https://docs.rs/parsing/index.html)

`parsing`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [flags](https://docs.rs/flags/index.html)
- Helpers to handle AMQP flags.
- [generation](https://docs.rs/generation/index.html)
- Generation utilities for the various AMQP types.
- [parsing](https://docs.rs/parsing/index.html)
- Parsing utilities for the various AMQP types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Byte](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteArray.html)- Array
- An array of bytes (RabbitMQ specific)
- [Decimal](https://docs.rs/struct.DecimalValue.html)- Value
- A Decimal value composed of a scale and a value
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldArray.html)- Array
- An array of AMQPValue
- [Field](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldTable.html)- Table
- A Map<String, AMQPValue>
- [Long](https://docs.rs/struct.LongString.html)- String
- A String
- [Short](https://docs.rs/struct.ShortString.html)- String
- A String (deprecated)
- [Short](https://docs.rs/struct.ShortStringError.html)- String - Error
- Error returned when constructing a [ShortString](https://docs.rs/struct.ShortString.html)from a string that exceeds[MAX_SHORT_STRING_LENGTH](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_SHORT_STRING_LENGTH.html)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/enum.AMQPType.html)- Type
- Enumeration referencing all the available AMQP types
- [AMQP](https://docs.rs/enum.AMQPValue.html)- Value
- Enumeration referencing the possible AMQP values depending on the types

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_SHORT_STRING_LENGTH.html)- SHORT_ - STRING_ - LENGTH
- Maximum byte length of a [ShortString](https://docs.rs/struct.ShortString.html)

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Boolean](https://docs.rs/type.Boolean.html)
- AMQP boolean (`t`): a single true/false value.
- [Channel](https://docs.rs/type.ChannelId.html)- Id
- A Channel identifier
- [Chunk](https://docs.rs/type.ChunkSize.html)- Size
- The size of a chunk of a delivery’s payload
- [Consumer](https://docs.rs/type.ConsumerCount.html)- Count
- The number of consumers
- [Delivery](https://docs.rs/type.DeliveryTag.html)- Tag
- A delivery tag
- [Double](https://docs.rs/type.Double.html)
- AMQP double (`d`): a 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point value.
- [Float](https://docs.rs/type.Float.html)

- AMQP long-long-int (`L`): a signed 64-bit integer.

- AMQP long-uint (`i`): an unsigned 32-bit integer.

- The number of messages

- The size of a delivery’s payload

- A reply code (for closing channels and connections)

# percent_encoding - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/percent-encoding/^2.0/

## Expand description

URLs use special characters to indicate the parts of the request.
For example, a `?` question mark marks the end of a path and the start of a query string.
In order for that character to exist inside a path, it needs to be encoded differently.

Percent encoding replaces reserved characters with the `%` escape character
followed by a byte value as two hexadecimal digits.
For example, an ASCII space is replaced with `%20`.

When encoding, the set of characters that can (and should, for readability) be left alone
depends on the context.
The `?` question mark mentioned above is not a separator when used literally
inside of a query string, and therefore does not need to be encoded.
The [ AsciiSet](https://docs.rs/struct.AsciiSet.html) parameter of

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.percent_encode.html)

`percent_encode`[lets callers configure this.](https://docs.rs/fn.utf8_percent_encode.html)

`utf8_percent_encode`This crate deliberately does not provide many different sets.
Users should consider in what context the encoded string will be used,
read relevant specifications, and define their own set.
This is done by using the `add` method of an existing set.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use percent_encoding::{utf8_percent_encode, AsciiSet, CONTROLS};
/// https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#fragment-percent-encode-set
const FRAGMENT: &AsciiSet = &CONTROLS.add(b' ').add(b'"').add(b'<').add(b'>').add(b'`');
assert_eq!(utf8_percent_encode("foo <bar>", FRAGMENT).to_string(), "foo%20%3Cbar%3E");
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ascii](https://docs.rs/struct.AsciiSet.html)- Set
- Represents a set of characters or bytes in the ASCII range.
- [Percent](https://docs.rs/struct.PercentDecode.html)- Decode
- The return type of `percent_decode`
- [Percent](https://docs.rs/struct.PercentEncode.html)- Encode
- The return type of `percent_encode``utf8_percent_encode`

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CONTROLS](https://docs.rs/constant.CONTROLS.html)
- The set of 0x00 to 0x1F (C0 controls), and 0x7F (DEL).
- [NON_](https://docs.rs/constant.NON_ALPHANUMERIC.html)- ALPHANUMERIC
- Everything that is not an ASCII letter or digit.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [percent_](https://docs.rs/fn.percent_decode.html)- decode
- Percent-decode the given bytes.
- [percent_](https://docs.rs/fn.percent_decode_str.html)- decode_ - str
- Percent-decode the given string.
- [percent_](https://docs.rs/fn.percent_encode.html)- encode
- Percent-encode the given bytes with the given set.
- [percent_](https://docs.rs/fn.percent_encode_byte.html)- encode_ - byte
- Return the percent-encoding of the given byte.
- [utf8_](https://docs.rs/fn.utf8_percent_encode.html)- percent_ - encode
- Percent-encode the UTF-8 encoding of the given string.

# url - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/url/^2.0/

## Expand description

rust-url is an implementation of the [URL Standard](http://url.spec.whatwg.org/)
for the [Rust](http://rust-lang.org/) programming language.

[§](https://docs.rs#url-parsing-and-data-structures)URL parsing and data structures

First, URL parsing may fail for various reasons and therefore returns a `Result`.

```
use url::{Url, ParseError};
assert!(Url::parse("http://[:::1]") == Err(ParseError::InvalidIpv6Address))
```
Let’s parse a valid URL and look at its components.

```
use url::{Url, Host, Position};
let issue_list_url = Url::parse(
    "https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues?labels=E-easy&state=open"
)?;
assert!(issue_list_url.scheme() == "https");
assert!(issue_list_url.username() == "");
assert!(issue_list_url.password() == None);
assert!(issue_list_url.host_str() == Some("github.com"));
assert!(issue_list_url.host() == Some(Host::Domain("github.com")));
assert!(issue_list_url.port() == None);
assert!(issue_list_url.path() == "/rust-lang/rust/issues");
assert!(issue_list_url.path_segments().map(|c| c.collect::<Vec<_>>()) ==
        Some(vec!["rust-lang", "rust", "issues"]));
assert!(issue_list_url.query() == Some("labels=E-easy&state=open"));
assert!(&issue_list_url[Position::BeforePath..] == "/rust-lang/rust/issues?labels=E-easy&state=open");
assert!(issue_list_url.fragment() == None);
assert!(!issue_list_url.cannot_be_a_base());
```
Some URLs are said to be *cannot-be-a-base*:
they don’t have a username, password, host, or port,
and their “path” is an arbitrary string rather than slash-separated segments:

```
use url::Url;
let data_url = Url::parse("data:text/plain,Hello?World#")?;
assert!(data_url.cannot_be_a_base());
assert!(data_url.scheme() == "data");
assert!(data_url.path() == "text/plain,Hello");
assert!(data_url.path_segments().is_none());
assert!(data_url.query() == Some("World"));
assert!(data_url.fragment() == Some(""));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#default-features)Default Features

Versions `<= 2.5.2` of the crate have no default features. Versions `> 2.5.2` have the default feature ‘std’.
If you are upgrading across this boundary and you have specified `default-features = false`, then
you will need to add the ‘std’ feature or the ‘alloc’ feature to your dependency.
The ‘std’ feature has the same behavior as the previous versions. The ‘alloc’ feature
provides no_std support.

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Enable the `serde` feature to include `Deserialize` and `Serialize` implementations for `url::Url`.

[§](https://docs.rs#base-url)Base URL

Many contexts allow URL *references* that can be relative to a *base URL*:

`<link rel="stylesheet" href="../main.css">`Since parsed URLs are absolute, giving a base is required for parsing relative URLs:

```
use url::{Url, ParseError};
assert!(Url::parse("../main.css") == Err(ParseError::RelativeUrlWithoutBase))
```
Use the `join` method on an `Url` to use it as a base URL:

```
use url::Url;
let this_document = Url::parse("http://servo.github.io/rust-url/url/index.html")?;
let css_url = this_document.join("../main.css")?;
assert_eq!(css_url.as_str(), "http://servo.github.io/rust-url/main.css");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-serde)Feature: `serde`

If you enable the `serde` feature, [ Url](https://docs.rs/struct.Url.html) will implement

[and](https://docs.rs/serde/1/serde/trait.Serialize.html)

`serde::Serialize`[. See](https://docs.rs/serde/1/serde/trait.Deserialize.html)

`serde::Deserialize`[serde documentation](https://serde.rs)for more information.

`url = { version = "2", features = ["serde"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#feature-debugger_visualizer)Feature: `debugger_visualizer`

If you enable the `debugger_visualizer` feature, the `url` crate will include
a [natvis file](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/debugger/create-custom-views-of-native-objects)
for [Visual Studio](https://www.visualstudio.com/) that allows you to view
[ Url](https://docs.rs/struct.Url.html) objects in the debugger.

This feature requires Rust 1.71 or later.

`url = { version = "2", features = ["debugger_visualizer"] }`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [form_urlencoded](https://docs.rs/form_urlencoded/1.2.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/form_urlencoded/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Opaque](https://docs.rs/struct.OpaqueOrigin.html)- Origin
- Opaque identifier for URLs that have file or other schemes
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseOptions.html)- Options
- Full configuration for the URL parser.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.PathSegmentsMut.html)- Segments - Mut
- Exposes methods to manipulate the path of an URL that is not cannot-be-base.
- [Url](https://docs.rs/struct.Url.html)
- A parsed URL record.
- [UrlQuery](https://docs.rs/struct.UrlQuery.html)
- Implementation detail of `Url::query_pairs_mut`. Typically not used directly.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Host](https://docs.rs/enum.Host.html)
- The host name of an URL.
- [Origin](https://docs.rs/enum.Origin.html)
- The origin of an URL
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- Errors that can occur during parsing.
- [Position](https://docs.rs/enum.Position.html)
- Indicates a position within a URL based on its components.
- [Syntax](https://docs.rs/enum.SyntaxViolation.html)- Violation
- Non-fatal syntax violations that can occur during parsing.

Delegate all authentication to the transport instead of the RabbitMQ server

# async-rs 0.8.11 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-rs/0.8.11

**A Rust async runtime abstraction library.**

Provides a unified `Runtime` enum and a `traits` module (`Executor`, `Reactor`,
`Dns`, …) that abstract over Tokio, smol, and async-global-executor.
Applications select exactly one runtime via feature flags; library crates
depend on the trait objects and remain runtime-agnostic.

## Feature flags

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `tokio`(default) | Tokio runtime |
| `smol` | smol executor |
| `async-global-executor` | async-global-executor |
| `async-io` | async-io reactor (required by `smol`) |
| `hickory-dns` | Hickory DNS resolver (tokio only) |

## Example

```
use ;
use ;
async
async
async
```

# async_compat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-compat/^0.2.5/

## Expand description

Compatibility adapter between tokio and futures.

There are two kinds of compatibility issues between [tokio](https://docs.rs/tokio) and [futures](https://docs.rs/futures):

- Tokio’s types cannot be used outside tokio context, so any attempt to use them will panic.
- Solution: If you apply the `Compat`*not*mean the future is polled by the tokio runtime - it only means the future sets a thread-local variable pointing to the global tokio runtime so that tokio’s types can be used inside it.

- Solution: If you apply the
- Tokio and futures have similar but different I/O traits `AsyncRead`,`AsyncWrite`,`AsyncBufRead`, and`AsyncSeek`.- Solution: When the `Compat`

- Solution: When the

You can apply the [ Compat](https://docs.rs/struct.Compat.html) adapter using the

[constructor or using any method from the](https://docs.rs/struct.Compat.html#method.new)

`Compat::new()`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.CompatExt.html)

`CompatExt`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

This program reads lines from stdin and echoes them into stdout, except it’s not going to work:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    futures::executor::block_on(async {
        let stdin = tokio::io::stdin();
        let mut stdout = tokio::io::stdout();
        // The following line will not work for two reasons:
        // 1. Runtime error because stdin and stdout are used outside tokio context.
        // 2. Compilation error due to mismatched `AsyncRead` and `AsyncWrite` traits.
        futures::io::copy(stdin, &mut stdout).await?;
        Ok(())
    })
}
```
To get around the compatibility issues, apply the [ Compat](https://docs.rs/struct.Compat.html) adapter to

`stdin`, `stdout`, and
[:](https://docs.rs/futures/0.3/futures/io/fn.copy.html)

`futures::io::copy()````
use async_compat::CompatExt;
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    futures::executor::block_on(async {
        let stdin = tokio::io::stdin();
        let mut stdout = tokio::io::stdout();
        futures::io::copy(stdin.compat(), &mut stdout.compat_mut()).compat().await?;
        Ok(())
    })
}
```
It is also possible to apply [ Compat](https://docs.rs/struct.Compat.html) to the outer future passed to

[rather than](https://docs.rs/futures/0.3/futures/executor/fn.block_on.html)

`futures::executor::block_on()`[itself. When applied to the outer future, individual inner futures don’t need the adapter because they’re all now inside tokio context:](https://docs.rs/futures/0.3/futures/io/fn.copy.html)

`futures::io::copy()````
use async_compat::{Compat, CompatExt};
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    futures::executor::block_on(Compat::new(async {
        let stdin = tokio::io::stdin();
        let mut stdout = tokio::io::stdout();
        futures::io::copy(stdin.compat(), &mut stdout.compat_mut()).await?;
        Ok(())
    }))
}
```
The compatibility adapter converts between tokio-based and futures-based I/O types in any direction. Here’s how we can write the same program by using futures-based I/O types inside tokio:

```
use async_compat::CompatExt;
use blocking::Unblock;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let mut stdin = Unblock::new(std::io::stdin());
    let mut stdout = Unblock::new(std::io::stdout());
    tokio::io::copy(&mut stdin.compat_mut(), &mut stdout.compat_mut()).await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
Finally, we can use any tokio-based crate from any other async runtime.
Here are [reqwest](https://docs.rs/reqwest) and [warp](https://docs.rs/warp) as an example:

```
use async_compat::{Compat, CompatExt};
use warp::Filter;
fn main() {
    futures::executor::block_on(Compat::new(async {
        // Make an HTTP GET request.
        let response = reqwest::get("https://www.rust-lang.org").await.unwrap();
        println!("{}", response.text().await.unwrap());
        // Start an HTTP server.
        let routes = warp::any().map(|| "Hello from warp!");
        warp::serve(routes).run(([127, 0, 0, 1], 8080)).await;
    }))
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Compat](https://docs.rs/struct.Compat.html)
- Compatibility adapter for futures and I/O types.

# async_global_executor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-global-executor/^3.1/

## Expand description

A global executor built on top of async-executor and async_io

The global executor is lazily spawned on first use. It spawns as many threads
as the number of cpus by default. You can override this using the
`ASYNC_GLOBAL_EXECUTOR_THREADS` environment variable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
// spawn a task on the multi-threaded executor
let task1 = async_global_executor::spawn(async {
    1 + 2
});
// spawn a task on the local executor (same thread)
let task2 = async_global_executor::spawn_local(async {
    3 + 4
});
let task = future::zip(task1, task2);
// run the executor
async_global_executor::block_on(async {
    assert_eq!(task.await, (3, 7));
});
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Global](https://docs.rs/struct.GlobalExecutorConfig.html)- Executor - Config
- Configuration to init the thread pool for the multi-threaded global executor.
- [Task](https://docs.rs/struct.Task.html)
- A spawned task.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [block_](https://docs.rs/fn.block_on.html)- on
- Runs the global and the local executor on the current thread
- [init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html)
- Init the global executor, spawning as many threads as the number or cpus or
the value specified by the `ASYNC_GLOBAL_EXECUTOR_THREADS`environment variable if specified.
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_with_config.html)- with_ - config
- Init the global executor, spawning as many threads as specified or the value specified by the specified environment variable.
- [spawn](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn.html)
- Spawns a task onto the multi-threaded global executor.
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_blocking.html)- blocking
- Runs blocking code on a thread pool.
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_local.html)- local
- Spawns a task onto the local executor.
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_more_threads.html)- more_ - threads
- Spawn more executor threads, up to configured max value.
- [stop_](https://docs.rs/fn.stop_current_thread.html)- current_ - thread
- Stop the current executor thread, if we exceed the configured min value
- [stop_](https://docs.rs/fn.stop_thread.html)- thread
- Stop one of the executor threads, down to configured min value

# async_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-io/^2.0/

## Expand description

Async I/O and timers.

This crate provides two tools:

- `Async`- [many other](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-io/tree/master/examples)types) to use in async programs.
- `Timer`

For concrete async networking types built on top of this crate, see [ async-net](https://docs.rs/async-net).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

The first time [ Async](https://docs.rs/struct.Async.html) or

[is used, a thread named “async-io” will be spawned. The purpose of this thread is to wait for I/O events reported by the operating system, and then wake appropriate futures blocked on I/O or timers when they can be resumed.](https://docs.rs/struct.Timer.html)

`Timer`To wait for the next I/O event, the “async-io” thread uses [epoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epoll) on Linux/Android/illumos,
[kqueue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kqueue) on macOS/iOS/BSD, [event ports](https://illumos.org/man/port_create) on illumos/Solaris, and [IOCP](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/i-o-completion-ports) on Windows. That
functionality is provided by the [ polling](https://docs.rs/polling) crate.

However, note that you can also process I/O events and wake futures on any thread using the
[ block_on()](https://docs.rs/fn.block_on.html) function. The “async-io” thread is therefore just a fallback mechanism
processing I/O events in case no other threads are.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Connect to `example.com:80`, or time out after 10 seconds.

```
use async_io::{Async, Timer};
use futures_lite::{future::FutureExt, io};
use std::net::{TcpStream, ToSocketAddrs};
use std::time::Duration;
let addr = "example.com:80".to_socket_addrs()?.next().unwrap();
let stream = Async::<TcpStream>::connect(addr).or(async {
    Timer::after(Duration::from_secs(10)).await;
    Err(io::ErrorKind::TimedOut.into())
})
.await?;
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [os](https://docs.rs/os/index.html)
- Platform-specific functionality.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/struct.Async.html)
- Async adapter for I/O types.
- [Readable](https://docs.rs/struct.Readable.html)
- Future for `Async::readable`
- [Readable](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadableOwned.html)- Owned
- Future for `Async::readable_owned`
- [Timer](https://docs.rs/struct.Timer.html)
- A future or stream that emits timed events.
- [Writable](https://docs.rs/struct.Writable.html)
- Future for `Async::writable`
- [Writable](https://docs.rs/struct.WritableOwned.html)- Owned
- Future for `Async::writable_owned`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [IoSafe](https://docs.rs/trait.IoSafe.html)
- Types whose I/O trait implementations do not drop the underlying I/O source.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [block_](https://docs.rs/fn.block_on.html)- on
- Blocks the current thread on a future, processing I/O events when idle.

# async_trait - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-trait/^0.1.89/

## Expand description

#### Type erasure for async trait methods

The stabilization of async functions in traits in Rust 1.75 did not include
support for using traits containing async functions as `dyn Trait`. Trying
to use dyn with an async trait produces the following error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Trait` is not dyn compatible
 --> src/main.rs:5:22
  |
5 | pub fn make() -> Box<dyn Trait> {
  |                      ^^^^^^^^^ `Trait` is not dyn compatible
  |
note: for a trait to be dyn compatible it needs to allow building a vtable
      for more information, visit <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility>
 --> src/main.rs:2:14
  |
1 | pub trait Trait {
  |           ----- this trait is not dyn compatible...
2 |     async fn f(&self);
  |              ^ ...because method `f` is `async`
  = help: consider moving `f` to another trait
```
This crate provides an attribute macro to make async fn in traits work with dyn traits.

Please refer to [ why async fn in traits are hard](https://smallcultfollowing.com/babysteps/blog/2019/10/26/async-fn-in-traits-are-hard/) for a deeper
analysis of how this implementation differs from what the compiler and
language deliver natively.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example implements the core of a highly effective advertising platform using async fn in a trait.

The only thing to notice here is that we write an `#[async_trait]` macro on
top of traits and trait impls that contain async fn, and then they work. We
get to have `Vec<Box<dyn Advertisement + Sync>>` or `&[&dyn Advertisement]`,
for example.

```
use async_trait::async_trait;
#[async_trait]
trait Advertisement {
    async fn run(&self);
}
struct Modal;
#[async_trait]
impl Advertisement for Modal {
    async fn run(&self) {
        self.render_fullscreen().await;
        for _ in 0..4u16 {
            remind_user_to_join_mailing_list().await;
        }
        self.hide_for_now().await;
    }
}
struct AutoplayingVideo {
    media_url: String,
}
#[async_trait]
impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo {
    async fn run(&self) {
        let stream = connect(&self.media_url).await;
        stream.play().await;
        // Video probably persuaded user to join our mailing list!
        Modal.run().await;
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-features)Supported features

It is the intention that all features of Rust traits should work nicely with
#[async_trait], but the edge cases are numerous. Please file an issue if
you see unexpected borrow checker errors, type errors, or warnings. There is
no use of `unsafe` in the expanded code, so rest assured that if your code
compiles it can’t be that badly broken.

☑ Self by value, by reference, by mut reference, or no self;

☑ Any number of arguments, any return value;

☑ Generic type parameters and lifetime parameters;

☑ Associated types;

☑ Having async and non-async functions in the same trait;

☑ Default implementations provided by the trait;

☑ Elided lifetimes.

[§](https://docs.rs#explanation)Explanation

Async fns get transformed into methods that return `Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send + 'async_trait>>` and delegate to an async block.

For example the `impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo` above would be
expanded as:

```
impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo {
    fn run<'async_trait>(
        &'async_trait self,
    ) -> Pin<Box<dyn core::future::Future<Output = ()> + Send + 'async_trait>>
    where
        Self: Sync + 'async_trait,
    {
        Box::pin(async move {
            /* the original method body */
        })
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-threadsafe-futures)Non-threadsafe futures

Not all async traits need futures that are `dyn Future + Send`. To avoid
having Send and Sync bounds placed on the async trait methods, invoke the
async trait macro as `#[async_trait(?Send)]` on both the trait and the impl
blocks.

[§](https://docs.rs#elided-lifetimes)Elided lifetimes

Be aware that async fn syntax does not allow lifetime elision outside of `&`
and `&mut` references. (This is true even when not using #[async_trait].)
Lifetimes must be named or marked by the placeholder `'_`.

Fortunately the compiler is able to diagnose missing lifetimes with a good error message.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
type Elided<'a> = &'a usize;
#[async_trait]
trait Test {
    async fn test(not_okay: Elided, okay: &usize) {}
}
```
```
error[E0726]: implicit elided lifetime not allowed here
 --> src/main.rs:9:29
  |
9 |     async fn test(not_okay: Elided, okay: &usize) {}
  |                             ^^^^^^- help: indicate the anonymous lifetime: `<'_>`
```
The fix is to name the lifetime or use `'_`.

```
#[async_trait]
trait Test {
    // either
    async fn test<'e>(elided: Elided<'e>) {}
    // or
    async fn test(elided: Elided<'_>) {}
}
```

# futures_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-core/^0.3/

## Expand description

Core traits and types for asynchronous operations in Rust.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use self::future::`- [FusedFuture](https://docs.rs/future/trait.FusedFuture.html);
- `pub use self::future::`- [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html);
- `pub use self::future::`- [TryFuture](https://docs.rs/future/trait.TryFuture.html);
- `pub use self::stream::`- [FusedStream](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.FusedStream.html);
- `pub use self::stream::`- [Stream](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.Stream.html);
- `pub use self::stream::`- [TryStream](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.TryStream.html);
